sections.text:
* Correspondence: ruishengdiao@intl.zju.edu.cn
Abstract
With the strategic advancement of energy structure transformation and the implementation
of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals, the Integrated Energy System (IES) has
become a core research direction owing to its superior performance in multi-energy com-
plementation, operational efficiency, and low-carbon emission characteristics. Nevertheless,
existing studies reveal that the optimal operation of IES still faces significant challenges,
including the high complexity of multi-energy coupling, supply–demand imbalance caused
by renewable energy penetration, and insufficient exploitation of demand-side flexibil-
ity. As a core measure of demand-side management, demand response (DR) provides
an effective approach to motivate users to adjust power load via price incentives or di-
rect load control. DR can effectively smooth load profiles, improve resource utilization,
and boost the consumption level of renewable energy. To meet the operational demands
of modern IES, this paper establishes a security-constrained economic dispatch model
embedded with multi-level demand response mechanisms. The proposed framework is
divided into four key modules: First, a price-based demand response strategy is developed
to dynamically guide users in regulating multi-energy consumption behaviors. Second,
electric vehicles (EVs) are considered flexible demand-side resources with unique response
characteristics. An aggregated EV charging–discharging model is established to suppress
power fluctuations and support high proportions of renewable energy integration. Third, to
precisely calculate the overall operating cost of IES, a combined economic evaluation index
integrating time-of-use tariff and Levelized Cost of Electricity is adopted. It maintains a
balance between amortized long-term generation investment and short-term operational
expenditure, and coordinates the economic benefits and operational reliability of the whole
system. Finally, numerical simulations are performed on a coupled test system comprising
an IEEE 33-bus distribution network and a 20-node natural gas network. Simulation re-
sults verify that the proposed co-optimization model can effectively reduce total system
operating costs and greatly improve the local assumption of fluctuating renewable energy.
Keywords: integrated energy system; demand response; vehicle-to-grid; renewable energy
integration; economic dispatch

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Driven by the goals of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality, the global energy struc-
ture is undergoing a profound transition from a centralized fossil-fuel-dominated paradigm
Energies 2026, 19, 3238 https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143238
Energies 2026, 19, 3238 2 of 33
to a decarbonized, distributed, and multi-vector configuration [1]. Against this backdrop,
the Integrated Energy System (IES) has gained traction as an infrastructure that ties electric-
ity, natural gas, heat, and cooling into one framework; because these carriers are coupled
and energy can be converted across them, resources are used in cascade rather than carrier
by carrier [2]. Compared with conventional decoupled energy networks, the IES offers
significant advantages in accommodating renewable energy, achieving comprehensive
energy efficiency, and reducing carbon emissions [ 3]. However, the high proportion of
integration of fluctuating renewables, the strong nonlinear coupling among diverse energy
carriers, and the insufficient exploitation of demand-side flexibility have posed significant
challenges to the secure and economic operation of the IES [ 4]. Therefore, developing a
coordinated co-optimization scheduling framework that fully unlocks supply-side and
demand-side flexibility has become a research focus in recent years [5].
As a core measure of demand-side management, demand response (DR) provides
an effective approach to motivate end users to actively regulate their energy consump-
tion through price incentives or direct load control [6]. Among various DR mechanisms,
price-based demand response (PDR) guided by time-of-use (TOU) tariffs has been widely
adopted owing to its market compatibility, minimal administrative intervention, and broad
social acceptability [7]. Reference [8] established a TOU pricing model based on a cross-
price elasticity matrix to characterize consumers’ multi-period, interdependent response
behaviors. In reference [9], a multi-energy PDR framework was developed for an IES opera-
tor, in which shiftable and interruptible loads were jointly scheduled to flatten the net-load
curve. Reference [10] proposed a dynamic TOU pricing mechanism that accounts for both
wholesale procurement cost volatility and peak-to-valley regulation, thereby improving
peak shaving performance. A Stackelberg game between the operator and multi-energy
consumers was solved in [11] to recover the optimal retail price vector, while [12] folded
renewable forecast uncertainty into a real-time pricing scheme so that flexible loads would
respond more sharply to scarcity. Taken together, these works confirm that PDR can re-
shape the load profile. What they share is a narrow treatment of the TOU price vector: it is
bounded but otherwise left free, and the constraints that keep the market itself stable—caps
on the peak-to-valley ratio, an enforced ordering of peak, flat, and valley tariffs—are rarely
written into the formulation, even though it is precisely these limits that protect social
welfare and head off clearing failures.
Alongside these stationary resources, the spread of electric vehicles (EVs) has turned
the vehicle-to-grid (V2G) concept into a fast-acting source of flexibility [ 13]. With bidi-
rectional chargers, an aggregated fleet behaves like distributed mobile storage: it soaks
up surplus renewable output overnight and returns energy to the grid when demand
peaks [14]. A series of modeling efforts builds on this idea. The aggregated dispatch model
in [15] represents the random arrival and departure of vehicles with normal distributions;
ref. [16] coordinates charging to damp wind fluctuations and curb curtailment; ref. [ 17]
studies V2G supplying ancillary services such as frequency regulation and spinning reserve
inside a distribution network; and [18] embeds V2G in microgrid energy management to
price the gains from two-way exchange. Comparing uncoordinated against coordinated
operation, ref. [19] then quantifies how V2G smooths load and steadies voltage. What these
studies have in common is that they stay almost entirely within the electrical subsystem,
and seldom ask how V2G flexibility travels into a coupled carrier—above all how it relieves
the gas network indirectly by trimming the peaking duty of gas turbines.
For the IES involving electricity and natural gas, cross-carrier coupling is primarily
achieved through Combined Heat and Power (CHP) units, gas-fired turbines, and power-
to-gas (P2G) facilities, which together form a bidirectional energy loop [20]. Reference [21]
formulated a joint optimal power–gas flow model and demonstrated that multi-energy co-
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143238
Energies 2026, 19, 3238 3 of 33
ordination can effectively mitigate localized congestion in both networks. In reference [22],
a P2G-based mechanism was developed to convert surplus wind generation into synthetic
natural gas, achieving deep renewable accommodation. A security-constrained co-dispatch
framework in [23] writes the Weymouth pipeline-flow equation directly into the problem,
and [24] goes a step further, carrying the gas network’s multi-period nodal pressures and
line-pack behavior into a day-ahead schedule; ref. [25] then layers on renewable uncertainty
and gas-source production limits. So, the physical electricity–gas coupling is modeled in
steadily finer detail, yet the demand side stays underexplored—in particular, how PDR
and V2G act together to relax the stress that accumulates between the two networks.
On the methodological side, IES scheduling is most often cast as a mixed-integer linear
program (MILP), which solves reliably and runs on off-the-shelf commercial solvers [26].
Nonlinear terms—the Weymouth gas-flow relation and the quadratic generator cost
curves—are handled through piecewise linearization, keeping the model within reach
of those solvers [27]. From the economic evaluation perspective, conventional dispatch
models often consider only short-term operational expenditures while neglecting the lifecy-
cle degradation of capital-intensive assets such as electrochemical energy storage systems
(EESS). To address this issue, the Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) framework has been
introduced to amortize lifecycle capital and maintenance expenditures over the asset oper-
ating horizon [28]. Reference [29] integrated LCOE-based depreciation costs for EESS into
a day-ahead dispatch model to prevent overly optimistic charging–discharging schedules.
Nevertheless, few studies have combined the LCOE evaluation with both TOU-based PDR
and V2G coordination under a unified electricity–gas IES scheduling framework.
In response to the above analyses, this paper establishes a security-constrained eco-
nomic co-optimization scheduling model for a coupled electricity–gas IES that embeds
multi-level demand-side flexibility mechanisms. A TOU-based PDR strategy that considers
cross-price elasticities and market stability constraints is developed to dynamically reshape
multi-energy consumption profiles. An aggregated V2G model with stochastic mobility
patterns is developed to exploit the bidirectional flexibility of EV fleets. A combined eco-
nomic evaluation index integrating TOU tariff and LCOE is adopted to balance short-term
operational expenditure and long-term asset depreciation. The main contributions of this
paper are summarized as follows.
(1) Under a coupled power–gas IES architecture, the synergistic interaction between PDR
and V2G is comprehensively considered, which fully unlocks demand-side flexibility
and coordinates the supply–demand balance across electricity and natural gas vectors.
(2) The PDR framework rests on a TOU tariff and a cross-price elasticity description of
user behavior, but unlike most formulations it is fenced in by explicit market-stability
constraints: the peak, flat, and valley tariffs must keep their ordering, and the peak-
to-valley ratio is held within fixed bounds. User adaptation is therefore captured
mathematically without let

sections.title: 2.1 Operator Architecture and Energy Flow Model for IES
2.1.1 Structure of the IES Operator
sections.text:
The Integrated Energy System (IES), serving as a crucial physical paradigm of the mod-
ern Energy Internet, is an advanced energy infrastructure that organically synthesizes the
production, transmission, storage, and consumption of diverse energy vectors—including
electricity, thermal energy, natural gas, and cooling power—via highly interconnected
physical distribution and transmission multi-networks, thereby achieving cross-carrier
multi-energy synergy, cascade utilization, and low-carbon transformations. Inside this
system, the IES Operator (IESO) is the entity that actually runs things: it manages the
internal co-dispatch, decides how the multi-carrier coupling components are configured,
and handles clearing and settlement in the retail energy markets. Its makeup is corre-
spondingly broad, spanning source-side input interfaces, the cross-carrier conversion grids,
hybrid storage banks, terminal load-control systems, and a Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS)
management center. This is a departure from the older picture of an isolated power or gas
dispatcher; the operator now aggregates several energy streams at once, converts among
them, coordinates the network as a whole, and matches supply to end-use demand as
conditions change. By dissolving the physical and managerial divisions that come with
running each carrier on its own, the IESO becomes a single digital control entity with
unified dispatch authority—which in turn hardens the system against the shocks of high
renewable penetration and opens room to develop the multi-energy market.
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143238
Energies 2026, 19, 3238 5 of 33

sections.title: 2.1.2 Analysis of Internal Energy Flow and Coupling Characteristics
sections.text:
Complex nonlinear coupling and multi-form transformations among electricity, heat,
gas, and cooling vectors across spatiotemporal scales interweave within the IES’s internal
architecture as shown as Figure 1. On the energy input side, the IES exhibits strong
inclusivity, accommodating diverse multi-energy streams from upstream wholesale markets
and natural energy networks. These include highly stochastic, volatile clean power from
wind turbines and photovoltaic arrays; thermal energy harvested from gas boilers; deep
geothermal resources; and industrial waste heat recovery systems, as well as natural
gas sourced from primary high-pressure pipelines. During the internal conversion stage,
various multi-energy converters serve as physical nodes for energy transmission. Take
electric heat pumps (HPs): their high coefficient of performance (COP) lets high-grade
electricity be turned into heat or cooling at low loss. Power-to-gas (P2G) units run in the
opposite direction, drawing on surplus or cheaply curtailed wind and solar to electrolyze
water and convert the resulting hydrogen, which opens a reverse path from electricity
back to gas and lets energy move across the two grids. Combined Heat and Power (CHP)
units consume natural gas to generate high-grade electricity and usable thermal energy
simultaneously, serving as core devices for multi-energy coupling. Absorption chillers
further recover high-temperature waste heat from CHPs or boilers to produce cooling
energy, realizing cascade utilization of thermal energy for cooling supply. On the energy
storage and regulation side, the system organically integrates a hybrid energy storage
system comprising lithium-ion batteries, vanadium redox flow batteries, hot water tanks,
ice storage tanks, and underground gas storage caverns, thereby extending the temporal
flexibility of energy dispatch. On the terminal demand side, load profiles cover highly
interruptible heavy industrial loads, shiftable thermal and cooling loads with strong thermal
inertia, and spatially movable Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) bidirectional charging piles. The
inherent temporal inertia of thermal and gas energy, coupled with multi-dimensional
spatial energy conversions, defines the physical boundaries and mathematical constraints
for internal energy flow optimization [30].
 
 
Figure 1. The structure of the IES.

sections.title: 2.2 TOU Pricing Mechanism Considering Energy Procurement Cost
2.2.1 Upstream Energy Procurement Cost Mechanism
sections.text:
The IES operator acts simultaneously as a wholesale-side buyer and a retail-side
seller within the energy value chain. On the wholesale trade front, the operator faces
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143238
Energies 2026, 19, 3238 6 of 33
diverse procurement cost variations driven by external bulk power grid spot markets, long-
term high-pressure natural gas pipeline contracts, and dynamic multi-energy commodity
markets. Procurement on the power side is volatile, tracking day-ahead spot clearing
prices, real-time balancing charges, and capacity-based network tariffs at the same time.
When demand peaks or renewable output runs low, the day-ahead price climbs steeply; on
windy nights, with wind plentiful, it collapses. Upstream natural gas procurement costs
are governed by a hybrid weighted combination of long-term pipeline capacity contract
prices and dynamic spot gas prices, exhibiting nonlinear stepped fluctuations subject to gas
pipeline pressure constraints. To mathematically solve the system dispatch problem over a

sections.title: 2.2.2 Downstream TOU-Based Load Regulation Framework for Operators
sections.text:
To efficiently transfer wholesale-side spot price volatility, operational cost pressures,
and physical renewable supply–demand imbalances down to terminal consumption
layers—while unleashing the latent cross-carrier flexibility of multi-energy complemen-
tary optimization—the operator must construct an adaptive retail-side TOU pricing and
multi-energy load regulation framework. This framework centers on customized retail
TOU electricity tariffs, accompanied by temporally coordinated retail TOU gas and ther-
mal price matrices. By deep mining historical multi-energy load big data and upstream
spot-clearing patterns, the operator segments the 24 h horizon into peak, flat, and valley
blocks. Daytime hours, when commercial load and procurement cost are both high, fall
into the peak band; the quiet overnight hours, when wind is abundant, become the valley.
Widening the gap between the two prices is what gives the tariff its bite. A high peak rate,
switched on when bulk power is tight or procurement turns expensive, pushes users to
trim flexible load or postpone it, while a low valley rate, released during heavy curtailment
or the overnight trough, pulls demand the other way. Underneath sits the usual digital
layer—smart grids, an automated Advanced Distribution Management System, an Energy
Management System (EMS), and dense Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI)—which
tracks the power, heat, and gas use of each user in a closed loop and keeps the physical,
information, and price flows tied together for the sake of flexibility and grid stability.
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143238
Energies 2026, 19, 3238 7 of 33

sections.title: 2.3 TOU-Based PDR Framework
sections.text:
Putting price-based demand response (PDR) into practice inside the IES means co-
ordinating flexible resources through prices rather than commands: the operator sets
multi-carrier retail price vectors and lets the market do the balancing. The idea rests on
one mathematical object, the cross-price elasticity matrix, which encodes how end-users
respond economically to those prices. Demand response then closes a loop between grid
and consumer, and the price elasticity of demand is what measures the strength of that
two-way link.
In concrete terms, the price elasticity of demand measures how far load moves for a
given change in commodity price over a period, and is written as
ε = ∆P/P0

P0 and λ0 are the baseline load demand and the initial energy price prior to demand

across other operational intervals throughout the day. To accurately capture these multi-

cross-price elasticity coefficient is introduced. The cross-price elasticity of demand reflects
the sensitivity of the demand quantity in a given period to the price variations in another

On a practical spatiotemporal operational plane, this multi-energy response manifests
through three highly complementary dimensions:
1. Temporal shifting and adaptive curtailment of flexible multi-carrier loads: Upon
observing premium retail peak power tariffs during industrial peak hours, large-
scale industrial microgrids automatically reduce the direct current of their smelting
cells; commercial facilities simultaneously utilize the structural thermal inertia of
modern smart buildings to actively scale down HVAC compressor power during peak
intervals, smoothly deferring these large thermal-driven power loads to nighttime
valley periods with ultra-low energy prices.
2. Cross-carrier substitution between energy vectors: Where heat can be met either
electrically or by gas, the choice follows price. If daytime power prices jump while
gas tariffs hold steady, a dual-fuel consumer backs off its electric heat pumps and
heats with a gas boiler or CHP instead; when wind floods the system overnight and
power turns cheap, the same consumer drops gas and heats electrically. The swap is
horizontal, carrier for carrier, and driven by the retail tariff alone.
The cross-price elasticity matrix is not estimated afresh in this study; its self- and
cross-elasticity entries are adopted from the established demand response literature for
electricity end-uses and are treated as exogenous parameters representative of a price-
responsive commercial, residential mix, which an operator would in practice calibrate from
historical smart-meter and tariff records by regressing observed load on price. Realism and
user acceptability are preserved not through the elasticity values alone but through the
bounds imposed on the response. User comfort and the limited willingness to participate
are captured by capping

sections.title: 3 Mathematical Modeling and Constraints
sections.text:
To prevent any ambiguity arising from the term “two-stage,” the proposed framework
is organized into two sequentially coupled decision stages that share the same 24 h day-
ahead horizon at hourly resolution but differ in their decision variables and information
sets, as summarized in Figure 2. In the first stage, the retail-pricing and demand-shaping
stage, the IES operator determines the time-of-use retail price vector for the peak, flat, and
valley blocks subject to the market-stability constraints of Section 3.2.1; acting through
the cross-price elasticity matrix, this price vector yields the price-responsive shiftable and
interruptible load. The settled price vector and the resulting post-PDR nodal load are the
first-stage decision variables and are passed downward as fixed boundary conditions. In
the second stage, the security-constrained dispatch stage, taking the reshaped load as the
boundary condition, the operator co-optimizes the dispatch of conventional and gas-fired
units, CHP and P2G plants, the EESS, and the bidirectional V2G fleet, together with the cou-
pled electricity- and gas-network constraints, so as to minimize the total operating cost. The
two stages are coupled through a one-directional price-to-load information flow: the first
stage decides how much demand to move and at what price, and the second stage decides
how to serve the resulting demand securely and economically. Because the user response
is endogenous to the pricing decision and both stages share the same day-ahead time
scale, they are assembled and solved as a single mixed-integer linear programming (MILP)
instance rather than by an iterative master–subproblem decomposition; this preserves
global optimality while retaining the conceptual two-stage decision logic. The second stage
therefore plays the role of the recourse-like dispatch layer that realizes the price decision
rather than a separate real-time correction.
Figure 2. Information flow of the proposed two-stage coordinated dispatch framework.

multi-carrier energy coupling, this study establishes an economic-optimal scheduling
model with the core objective of minimizing the system’s total operational cost within a
day-ahead scheduling horizon. This objective function not only coordinates the synergetic
procurement of multi-carrier energy flows on the wholesale side but also mathematically
captures the nonlinear energy-consumption characteristics of multi-energy conversion

CHP unit and the u-th gas-fired plant at time slot t (kW), respectively; Pp,t represents the
active electrical power input consumed by the p-th P2G device at time slot t (kW); ah, bh, ch
and au, bu, cu are the quadratic, linear, and constant cost coefficients governing the fuel
consumption and O&M expenses of the CHP and gas plants, respectively; and Cp signifies
the unit O&M cost coefficient of the P2G facilities (RMB/kWh).
The electrochemical energy storage system (EESS) lifecycle cost explicitly maps the im-
plicit costs of physical degradation, cycle-life degradation, and internal chemical efficiency
losses using Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) principles, thereby preventing aggressive
or overly optimistic scheduling profiles resulting from idealized modeling. This cost com-
ponent is quasi-linearized based on the discharge throughput over the dispatch horizon,
where CLCOE represents the levelized depreciation and maintenance cost coefficient of
the EESS (RMB/kWh), which comprehensively factors in the initial capital investment,
battery replacement costs, maximum cycle life, and salvage value; and Pout

sections.title: 3.2.1 TOU Pricing Vector and Market Stability Constraints
sections.text:
When designing or implementing retail TOU electricity pricing strategies, the grid
operator must systematically balance the regulatory efficacy of grid peak shaving with
social welfare and market financial sustainability. The peak tariff has to be high enough
to hold back demand when it matters most, but push it too far and consumer goodwill,
household budgets, and industrial output all suffer. The valley tariff faces the mirror
problem: low enough to pull load into the surplus hours, yet not so low that upstream
generators are starved of revenue. To keep the pricing vector from drifting into gouging,
welfare loss, or outright clearing failure, it is hemmed in by a set of tiered bounds.
First, the hierarchical relationship and absolute operational boundaries governing the
peak, flat, and valley electricity tariffs are mathematically constrained as follows:

sections.title: 3.2.2 Integrated Network Operational Constraints
sections.text:
Security, reliability, and thermodynamic efficiency in the co-optimized IES all
rest on a single constraint framework, which gathers the physical laws, operating en-
velopes, and technical limits of the electricity distribution grid and the gas transmission
network—two systems that are distinct in their physics yet tightly coupled in operation.
https://doi.org/10.3390/en19143238
Energies 2026, 19, 3238 13 of 33
The operational safe tracking of the electrical distribution grid is formulated using a
generalized branch-flow model. This multi-period framework encompasses distribution
network Distflow equations, transmission line thermal boundaries, nodal voltage/current
security margins, generator capacity limits, unit commitment and ramping restrictions, and
system-wide spinning reserve requirements.

The power balance conditions represent the strict application of the first law of ther-
modynamics to maintain system-wide power equilibrium. The voltage-drop relation does
the spatial counterpart: it links the voltages of neighboring buses and accounts for the
losses and drops that line impedance produces. With the Distflow constraints in force, the
grid is held in a secure operating state, resources are placed sensibly across the network,
and the chance of a local power mismatch or voltage excursion cascading into wider failure
is kept low.

sections.title: 5 Line Transmission Thermal Boundaries
sections.text:
Transmission limits exist to protect the physical line itself. Push the flow past a line’s
rated capacity and the overcurrent dumps excess Joule heat into the conductor; that heat
ages the insulation faster and makes phase-to-ground faults, mechanical damage, or fire
more likely. A badly overloaded line also drags down the voltage at downstream nodes,
and once that voltage falls below its nominal band, sensitive equipment misbehaves and
power quality suffers. Capping the active and reactive flows on each line keeps it clear of
thermal overload and preserves a safe transfer margin:

sections.title: 6 Nodal Voltage and Current Security Envelopes
sections.text:
Keeping nodal voltages and branch currents inside their local limits is central to grid
stability. When voltage sags too low, machines lose electromagnetic torque or are starved

high, the insulation in power electronics and transformers is overstressed, which ages it
prematurely or breaks it down outright. Currents matter for a different reason. Holding a
branch current within its continuous rating limits resistive loss, whereas an unbounded
current bleeds energy away as heat, raises operating cost, and shortens the life of the asset:

adjustment during transitional intervals, these constraints prevent severe mechanical fa-
tigue and thermal stress from aggressive load-following maneuvers. This extends the
service life of dispatchable units and ensures continuous, high-fidelity power tracking
across diverse grid conditions:

8 System Spinning Reserve Capacity Constraints
sections.text:
Reserve capacity constraints dictate that at any given hour within the dispatch horizon,
the cumulative residual generating capacity of all online synchronized units must strictly
exceed the system’s prevailing spinning reserve demand. This headroom is what lets the
IES ride out random disturbances. Real grids are routinely hit by the unexpected—a unit
trips, or load jumps—and with too little spinning reserve the balance breaks immediately,
forcing load shedding or, worse, a cascading blackout that takes economic and social costs
with it:
